full_text:
Subject:	Is it PhD research that you're doing?

Interviewer:	It is for my PhD but it's also for a funded project. I'm paid to work at the university as well to do this research funded by the ESRC, which is the Economic and Social Research Council. To look at why more women don't go into engineering basically but I’m also doing a PhD on the same subject at the same time.

Subject:	So how is it going so far?

Interviewer:	It's really good meeting everyone and seeing how they’re getting on with their placement and stuff like that. But the questions that I've got to ask relate to how you're getting on with your placement and how you think your placement relates to your degree and things like that. 

Subject:	When I was applying for a placement, it was really hard, I went to a lot of different interviews. I think I might have been for about twenty interviews, before I got an offer. This job it's about more on emission of fuels, research, like looking at fuels properties you know, but my degree is chemical engineering, so it doesn't really have anything related.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you've used, not necessarily your technical skills but other things you've learned off your course like, more general skills like communication skills and things like that. Do you think you've used things like that?

Subject:	I think yes, I think even though it doesn't have anything related I think it's really good because I've never worked before, so it's like good experience working with different people and people not my age, communicating with people not students. (Yes) Yes and I have learned quite a lot here like having to force myself to read all the technical reports that I can hardly understand, but it's like after a long practice maybe it's a good thing when I go back to uni when I read the chemistry books they will be easier to understand properly.

Interviewer:	Do you think you'll use what you're learning now when you back for your final year?

Subject:	I think some things are quite useful like the way I write reports. For example my supervisor said like I should write according to my audience, who's going to read my report. Then like each different report has different styles and those things I can apply when I go back to uni. And they offer a lot of different courses like just now I went for Microsoft PowerPoint course, so they have different courses you can go to.

Interviewer:	Ok is there anything that you wish you had learned at university before you came on placement that would have been helpful?

Subject:	Well because this work I'm doing has not much relation to my degree, so I think they could teach more on fuels or how we look at it, like the (catalytic cracking?) and all that. But we learn that in the A levels before. Maybe in the final year they're gonna - when you choose what stream you want to go to they'll teach more on that.

Interviewer:	Ok. Have you had to learn anything new on placement like dealing with different types of people like your boss, or customers, or clients or office politics or anything like that?

Subject:	Mm, yeah. There's something I find really confusing like the management system like this year they have changed the system like we are called the [name] Group but now they change it to the [name] Group, then they have like different targets and the new things that's been going on like you're coming to work and not only do you have to know what your projects are but you have to understand who's on these positions.

Interviewer:	It takes some getting used to.

Subject:	Yeah. And like reading journals, I have to do dissertation for [university] this year and my supervisor chose the title for me and that dissertation is also like a research that [company] is interested in. It’s er bio-fuels, it's like a hot topic in the petro-industry now, so it's really good.

Interviewer:	Were you taught anything about health and safety at the university?

Subject:	Not that much. It's, compared to where I’m working here it’s, like always about health and safety, but not as much at uni.

Interviewer:	Do you think it would be useful to do more at uni, to prepare you for coming here or do you think that there's enough health and safety training once you get here?

Subject:	Health and Safety training here, they're ok but at uni I don't really see a lot of health and safety going on. Before we go to the labs, like before we start to operate on the (pilot plants?) they don't seem to tell us how you have to be careful with them and unless it’s like really important. Like here even if you go up the stairs you have to hold the handrail.

Interviewer:	Ok do you think they should do more health and safety at university then or do you think it doesn't matter?

Subject:	It's better to explain about health and safety before you operate the plant, but like going up the stairs I don't think is relevant.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the university could have done more to prepare you for coming on placement?

Subject:	To help prepare me? I think because I didn't know before I accepted the place that I would actually be doing this kind of job and I asked my supervisor the other day, because they were interviewing my replacement for next year. (Ok) So I asked them if they had already seen the job description before they came and they said, “Yes, I'd sent it to them”. but I didn’t have a chance to look at it before when I came, so when I was in the interview then I realised oh this what I'm gonna do. Then when the people, the new students, came for interview I asked them if they'd seen it, they said that they hadn't seen it you know, so I don't whether it's the company's fault or the university's.

Interviewer:	Ok. How did you find the transition from being in education student to being at work, was it easy or difficult?

Subject:	Very difficult for the first month because I'm not used to getting up early. And, because I get a lift in, so I used to work the long hours with this girl that I know, she works from eight to five, which is normal working hours, I'm only supposed to work nine to five. Sometimes she works from eight to half-five, so it's like very long hours for me. At the start I'm not very used to it, but now I've found another lift that comes in at nine to five, but sometime when I have more work I would like to leave later.

Interviewer:	Ok, are you looking forward to going back to university?

Subject:	Yes, very. I don't know why maybe because well it's just not every day like coming to work and then only having weekends off, we get a lot more holiday. But, I’d like to be a student again.

Interviewer:	Are you keeping in touch with your friends and things like that?

Subject:	Yes

Interviewer:	Ok. What do you think are the main ways that work and university differ?

Subject:	The main . . .?

Interviewer:	The main differences between being at work and being at university?

Subject:	Like being at work, I think I feel - I think I feel more pressurised, like because, all of the work that I've done, it could be very important to the business, so I couldn't afford to make any mistakes. I have to do finances for my supervisor for his projects and they're like in million Euros, so if I like put one zero less, then they're gonna be all different, to draw the graph, second one and then to check for the exit budget, so at uni these things are not that important. They’re very different.

Interviewer:	Did you do anything on your course about finance or anything like that?

Subject:	We did process economics where, yes, you look at how you spend. That's quite different from what I'm doing, yes. I think like [name] and most of my classmates I talk to on placement now, I think most of the work they do are more chemical engineering based.

Interviewer:	Can you tell me a bit about what [company] do?

Subject:	Erm [company] sells fuel, they do a lot of different types of fuels, before I came I didn't realise it. They are very active in the F1. F1. Yes and then they have this new fuel, like automated fuel (sales?) are looking into.

Interviewer:	And your job involves looking at fuel emissions?

Subject:	Yes, fuel emissions, also bio-fuels. Just looking, I did erm, for this - there's this new alternative fuel called [name]. At the moment we only have the (pilot plant?) providing the new fuel, the new commercial plant is not gonna be ready until about a few years time and I look at how this - because we have a limited supply of it and it shows it to give really good emissions, like lower particulates, you know, so we look at how we choose which country to sell it. We sold it in Thailand because it's very bad pollution over there. (Yes) And then we sold it in Athens and not the whole of Greece, because we launched it with the Olympics to get like people (lost words) because Olympic games is always for a greener environment. Also we're looking at customers' feedback on that fuel. I helped my colleague to do research to write a report on all the customers' feedback on the new fuel.

Interviewer:	Is a lot of your time spent in the lab?

Subject:	No, I don't really do any lab work compared to with the other students here who spend all day in the lab but for me its more all reports and computer work.

Interviewer:	Ok. Does the company have like a programme or structure that placement students have to follow, like are there targets that you have set?

Subject:	Not really, but they do ask us what we want to achieve at the end of the year. It's very good in terms of that we can ask what we want to do, like if you want to get more involved in this certain project that you know of you can ask them for permission and then they’ll try to let you get involved in it.

Interviewer:	Yes, and you said you've been on quite a few training courses and things.

Subject:	Yes, and like because I studied chemical engineering I've always wanted to go to [name], the refinery next door and I've been for a few visits there to see how everything works.

Interviewer:	Ok, that sounds good. Do you feel like you do give an appropriate level of responsibility? 

Subject:	I think I'm alright, like sometimes when we don't have enough work to do, you can go around and ask for it, then you can help people, so that's alright, and when I have too much work I can just tell my supervisor what other works I have and can I do this first.

Interviewer:	So you have got quite a good relationship with your supervisor? He's quite approachable?

Subject:	Yes, and because they put me in the same room as him, so it' easier when I want something I just ask. They used to employ two students for my placement every year but this year we've got one, But because, they said it's good to have two they said because I can talk to the other students and discuss if I don't know anything or if the others or if the other student's better at doing something, so this year it's a bit harder but not too bad.

Interviewer:	Ok. Do [company] employ a lot of women?

Subject:	I think it's more men.

Interviewer:	In your section is it mostly men?

Subject:	Yes, in my section it's the fuel [name] so yes, the majority are men.

Interviewer:	Ok. How would you summarise your placement experience so far?

Subject:	I would think it's a good and different experience.

Interviewer:	What would you say have been the best and the worst things about it?

Subject:	The best thing - I don't think it's happened yet. When I finish my dissertation and be of more use to the company. Yes, it's not like I don't know want them to choose a title for me and then finish [inaudible] and didn’t help them in any way. The worst is maybe understanding emissions and fuel specifications. I think it's quite hard, because I have to go and visit the legislation websites and they're quite boring. I don't do any calculations that I do in uni, just more reading and understanding.

Interviewer:	Can it be a bit tedious sometimes?

Subject:	Yes, but its good practice.

Interviewer:	Has the placement met your expectations? Is there anything that you thought you would achieve but haven’t done yet?

Subject:	I would like to do more chemical engineering work like but that would be totally different from what I'm doing, so I don't think I'll be able to do that this year.

Interviewer:	What would you say now are the benefits of doing a placement?

Subject:	Getting to know people, to know how to communicate with different people, different age groups and also working is a totally different environment to studying.

Interviewer:	Do you think that'll help you when you go out into the workplace when you've finished university?

Subject:	Yes, I think there's one more thing as well. When they interview my replacement, they include me in their discussion like what do they want from this student and what do they think about that? So I can see from that point of view what the interviewers actually want to get out of the student. So that would help me, I think, when I actually go and find a job.

Interviewer:	Do you think there are any drawbacks to doing the placement?

Subject:	Not really. Despite the work is different from my degree but the other things are really good like you don't find a placement where you get mostly like a free lunch and a gym and a library. But there's also one more thing that this is quite far from town, like if you don't have a car like I don't, so it's really hard to come into work and to get a lift. Sometimes when you want to work later or you want to go to the gym you can't go because you have to get a lift. They don't do like a shuttle bus for the employees. That's one bad thing.

Interviewer:	How did you find moving to [town], was it difficult to begin with moving to a new place?

Subject:	It was not too bad, because I studied at [town] before I came to [university], so I moved from [town] to [town], so you get used to it.

Interviewer:	So you’re used to moving round?

Subject:	Yes

Interviewer:	Do you think that you have changed personally from doing the placement, like more confident or independent, things like that?

Subject:	Yes, I think it's sort of good practice for me to be speaking lots of English because I’m from Malaysia, you don't usually speak English like every day, every hour, this is good practice. And I think if I just go on to uni after my second year I won't see things like how I see things now.

Interviewer:	Would you recommend that other people did a placement?

Subject:	Yes I would.

Interviewer:	Would you recommend that people to do the placement that you're doing?

Subject:	It depends what they want to do after their uni and there are a lot of chemical engineer graduates in my department, they chose to do this work as in, it's also very technical but just like nothing to do with like walking around the refineries. It depends on the people.

Interviewer:	Is it a quite specialized area that you're in at the moment then?

Subject:	Yes, I spoke to my colleague, and she's a chemical engineer but she chose to work here. I asked her why she says its because she, it's very complicated at the refinery, like if you're a new starter, a new chemical engineer, you have to deal with operators, sometimes you want to change the way they operate but they won't listen and then you have to deal with it. That's why she chose to work and do research on, it's also on the products on what the refinery has produced but it's like a different side.

Interviewer:	Ok. You said that there were some other students on placement here I think?

Subject:	Yes but - no. I think that it's only two are of like fifteen those are the students, pre-university students, doing like a gap year. So there's only me and another girl who’s from Scotland.

Interviewer:	Do you think that you're treated equally, or the same as other placement students? 

Subject:	Yes, I think so yes.

Interviewer:	Do you think it's an advantage or disadvantage having other students on placement at the same time?

Subject:	It's an advantage because I have friends of my own age, at nearly my own age, and then all the students have lunch together, because we don't work in the same department we don't see each other in the day, so it's good to have lunch with different people and then work with different people, get to know more people.

Interviewer:	Do you support each other?

Subject:	Yes, yes, we do have like social gatherings you know, go out to the cinema.

Interviewer:	Ok that's good. Do you think that you’re treated the same as the permanent members of staff? Or are you treated like the student?

Subject:	Yes, we are sometimes, it depends on the work, like most of the time I am sort of treated like one of the permanent workers but some other times, like there was this bio fuels meeting that was on and my supervisor wanted me to go on it but then the speaker didn't allow me to go in it. He said, 'We don't allow students, we only allow [company] employees and then my supervisor didn't realise that, and she came and told me that they were talking about very confidential things about the company, about their findings and they didn't want to include me, so that's the difference sometimes.

Interviewer:	Is that frustrating?

Subject:	Yes, it is a bit yes.

Interviewer:	I think that confidentiality is a big issue for quite a lot of companies that interview some students working at [company] and they couldn't really tell me much about their jobs because of confidentiality (Alright) They weren't allowed to tell much about the company. But it's all confidential anyway.

Subject:	Yes but most of them, like if there's a talk or if there's a presentation, usually we do get to go.

Interviewer:	Have you had to do a lot of group or teamwork or is it mainly working by yourself?

Subject:	My supervisor did like a customer's report on that new fuel that we were supposed to do and he paired me with a colleague and we were supposed to do it together, which was good and now he has a new project and he paired me with a different colleague.

Interviewer:	Ok. How do you think doing group work at work compares with doing group work at university? Is it easier or harder? 

Subject:	At university there is usually – there’s not much of a difference. There's bigger groups of people working on the same thing, but here I've only been like in a group of two people. It’s not much of a difference, unless like in university you meet people who doesn’t do work like in a group, it's frustrating like that but here I don't think that's gonna happen because everyone is here to work or maybe they love their job, that's why they're here.

Interviewer:	Do you think that doing group work at university is beneficial for when you're doing group work here? Do you use skills from it?

Subject:	I do yes, like at uni, when you do group work you have to like listen to people's ideas and like try to accept it and it's the same as here as well, just listen and then you have to provide your own ideas if that's not done in group work at uni I might not know about it. 

Interviewer:	Ok. Have you particularly liked or disliked working with any people here?

Subject:	Not really - no.

Interviewer:	So it's just been okay?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Have you been given a mentor at all?

Subject:	No - mentor - are they the same as supervisors?

Interviewer:	Well sometimes I think a lot of people that haven't specifically been given a mentor see their supervisors as a mentor, but a mentor might be someone different, somewhere else in the company that you can just go and talk to about general things, if you had any problems or career advice or anything like that.

Subject:	There are different people for different things here, if I want, it depends, if I want to talk about a health and safety problem I could see a representative, or if I want to do some research in IT, there's an IT representative, I haven't got anyone that's especially assigned to me.

Interviewer:	If you need any advice or anything like that you would see your supervisor?

Subject:	Yes, my supervisor and the colleagues that I work with, that he paired me with, I know them as my friends as well, so I can talk to them.

Interviewer:	Yes, so they’re quite supportive, ok. Is there anyone else in the company or anyone in the company that you think of as like a role model? 

Subject:	I think one of the colleagues who I work with, she's a chemical engineer and she's only started like 6 months before me but when I came she's like catch up everything like that's going on really, she's been adapting really well and like understanding like all the different jargons that they use here - and every time I talk to her, because if I don't understand any work, she works for my supervisor, so if I don't understand any work that I'm doing I can just go to her and ask her and she'll explain it very clearly to me, so like talking to her sometimes like inspires me to work more hard, do more research. She's like a role model.

Interviewer:	Has anyone from the university been to visit you?

Subject:	No, no because I go back to university quite often. (Ok) So no, they've not been here to visit. My friends has been.

Interviewer:	But not a placement supervisor or anything like that?

Subject:	Oh yes, placement supervisor, he's been here once, once to visit me in September, that's two months after I started, he says he'll come about three times a year.

Interviewer:	Ok. What sort of things did they talk to you about?

Subject:	They talked to me about like how am I getting on and what other work that I do, he asked about my dissertation, how much time I allocate to do it a week and who are my supervisors who are looking after - because I have a different supervisor who looks after the dissertation.

Interviewer:	Did you know the person that came to visit you before? Did you know the person that came to visit?

Subject:	The lecturer? Yes. As in the name?

Interviewer:	Had they taught you at university?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Ok. Did they speak to your supervisor as well?

Subject:	Yes, I think they did spend some time with my supervisor and some time with me alone and with all of us.

Interviewer:	Did you find it helpful having that visit?

Subject:	It could be helpful if I had problems then I could talk to him more than my supervisor, but I find my supervisor quite friendly, so I can talk to him.

Interviewer:	So if you had any problems, you'd try and sort it out at work first before you went to your placement tutor?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Ok. Are you in contact with the person at university, when they're not visiting you, do they email you or anything like that?

Subject:	They don't really, no. I email him every month to send him the monthly report, I have to send a report every month to say what I'm doing.

Interviewer:	Would you be happy to talk to that person if you did have any problems at all? Or is there anyone else at university that you'd rather talk to?

Subject:	Maybe I would rather talk to my personal tutor at uni?

Interviewer:	Do you know whether, either here or at university, if they have like a complaints procedure if you did have any problems at all?

Subject:	I think there should be but not really.

Interviewer:	Ok. Are there appropriate facilities for women here? There's enough women toilets and if you had to wear, you probably don't, but if you have to wear safety clothing and things like that, is it in the right sizes?

Subject:	Oh yes, we had to do this fire fighting training where we had to like put out a fire. We had a red one, it was really big, but there are smaller sizes I think.

Interviewer:	Some of the students I’m interviewing are working on building sites and things like that, so they don't necessarily always have like women’s toilets?

Subject:	The fire extinguisher's so heavy I couldn’t even lift the lightest one, but it's my first time to put out a fire. [laughter]

Interviewer:	That sounds scary. 

Subject:	There's a properly trained firemen there to look after us - should be ok.

Interviewer:	Can you think of any occasions when you think of the fact that you're a woman has maybe determined reactions that you've got from people or anything like that?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	You feel like you're treated equally?

Subject:	Yes, yes. I think my supervisor prefers to have a girl student, because maybe the way we talk to people and the guys, I think, would seem a bit rude sometimes maybe.

Interviewer:	You mean that women are maybe be better at communicating?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Ok. Do you think that your career ambitions have changed since doing the placement?

Subject:	No I still want to be a chemical engineer.

Interviewer:	Do you know what area of chemical engineering you'd like to go into at all?

Subject:	I'd like to work in [name] if I can or I wanted to work for a pharmaceutical company before but now I think a petroleum company, it’s not bad.

Interviewer:	Would you work for [company] then, if you had that opportunity?

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Do you know whether they would let you come back if you wanted to?

Subject:	I don't know about that, I don't think so, I think I would have to apply again, because it's different companies, there are different small companies within [company].

Interviewer:	You wouldn't want to work in this area again?

Subject:	In the research department?

Interviewer:	Yes.

Subject:	No - I don't think so.

Interviewer:	Ok. Do you think that doing the placement will help you even if you go into another area?

Subject:	I think the communication skill would help, like knowing that you had to persuade the operators, or trying to make them see the sense of what you're doing. So, I think, speaking to all the different people here I think communication skills will help a lot.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the other section will be more male dominated than it is here or do you think it'll be the same?

Subject:	It feels more male dominated.

Interviewer:	Does that bother you at all?

Subject:	Not really.

Interviewer:	You said that the other girl said about it often being difficult trying to get the operators to do things, does that bother you at all?

Subject:	I don't think so, I think it’s like more challenging and more interesting, to think of different ways [laughter] I'll give it a go.

Interviewer:	I have got some questions now that are questions that I asked in the last interview but it's not a test, you see if you get the same answers, just to see if your opinion has changed from having the placement experience. And the first one is what five words would you use to describe, well I was going to say chemical engineering but I'll say the area that you've been working in at the minute. What five words would you use to describe it?

Subject:	It's different - The area I work in or the work that I do?

Interviewer:	Both, just like the characteristics of the general type of work that you’re doing.

Subject:	It’s - can I say technical? Erm…

Interviewer:	Do you think that the characteristics here would be different from the chemical engineering that you want to go into?

Subject:	The chemical engineering work also is very technical but it also involves a lot of reading, how you start up the plants and all the procedures. I'm interested to do what the chemical engineers do, so I'll find it more interesting maybe you know.

Interviewer:	Ok. Do you think that there are any advantages or disadvantages of being a woman in engineering?

Subject:	Advantages - Maybe if you do something wrong they won't penalise you that much. [laughter] 

Interviewer:	Has that happened to you, or is that just what you think?

Subject:	It’s what I think. Disadvantages might be – like some more difficult work, they might like give it to the guys, I think.

Interviewer:	Yes, ok. Does it concern you at all that there aren't more women in engineering? Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering? 

Subject:	Yes.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that they don't?

Subject:	Ah I think I remember my answer now, I think it’s going to be the same. I think because, for me as well like when we were small, women want to be like fashion designers, like all those feminine jobs, I would also like fashion, wear spiky heels and all that to work. But I think in becoming a chemical engineer or engineer, we do still go to work like normal people, like we do quite a lot of work on the computers as well but just like sometime you have to go down to the refineries, you have to wear the safety boots and all but I think it's something different from most people and I think it's good. I wouldn't like a job where you sit all day on a computer.

Interviewer:	So you like lots of variety?

Subject:	Yes, yes.

Interviewer:	I'm just looking at some things I wrote down from last time, one of them was that you maybe wanted to do a Master's course? Do you still think that you'd like to do that or would you just like to go straight to work when you've finished your degree?

Subject:	I am in a Master's course now.

Interviewer:	Oh you're doing the MEng.

Subject:	Yes, but I might just do the BEng because it's really expensive for me, for my parents because I pay international student fees, so that's the only reason, if my parents could afford it I think I'd like to study master's in chemical engineering, or later I might want to do a masters in management as well.

Interviewer:	Ok, that's everything, thank you very much, thank you for help.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Is it PhD research that you're doing?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It is for my PhD but it's also for a funded project. I'm paid to work at the university as well to do this research funded by the ESRC, which is the Economic and Social Research Council. To look at why more women don't go into engineering basically but I’m also doing a PhD on the same subject at the same time.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: So how is it going so far?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It's really good meeting everyone and seeing how they’re getting on with their placement and stuff like that. But the questions that I've got to ask relate to how you're getting on with your placement and how you think your placement relates to your degree and things like that.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: When I was applying for a placement, it was really hard, I went to a lot of different interviews. I think I might have been for about twenty interviews, before I got an offer. This job it's about more on emission of fuels, research, like looking at fuels properties you know, but my degree is chemical engineering, so it doesn't really have anything related.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you've used, not necessarily your technical skills but other things you've learned off your course like, more general skills like communication skills and things like that. Do you think you've used things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think yes, I think even though it doesn't have anything related I think it's really good because I've never worked before, so it's like good experience working with different people and people not my age, communicating with people not students. (Yes) Yes and I have learned quite a lot here like having to force myself to read all the technical reports that I can hardly understand, but it's like after a long practice maybe it's a good thing when I go back to uni when I read the chemistry books they will be easier to understand properly.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think you'll use what you're learning now when you back for your final year?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think some things are quite useful like the way I write reports. For example my supervisor said like I should write according to my audience, who's going to read my report. Then like each different report has different styles and those things I can apply when I go back to uni. And they offer a lot of different courses like just now I went for Microsoft PowerPoint course, so they have different courses you can go to.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok is there anything that you wish you had learned at university before you came on placement that would have been helpful?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well because this work I'm doing has not much relation to my degree, so I think they could teach more on fuels or how we look at it, like the (catalytic cracking?) and all that. But we learn that in the A levels before. Maybe in the final year they're gonna - when you choose what stream you want to go to they'll teach more on that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Have you had to learn anything new on placement like dealing with different types of people like your boss, or customers, or clients or office politics or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, yeah. There's something I find really confusing like the management system like this year they have changed the system like we are called the [name] Group but now they change it to the [name] Group, then they have like different targets and the new things that's been going on like you're coming to work and not only do you have to know what your projects are but you have to understand who's on these positions.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It takes some getting used to.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. And like reading journals, I have to do dissertation for [university] this year and my supervisor chose the title for me and that dissertation is also like a research that [company] is interested in. It’s er bio-fuels, it's like a hot topic in the petro-industry now, so it's really good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Were you taught anything about health and safety at the university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not that much. It's, compared to where I’m working here it’s, like always about health and safety, but not as much at uni.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it would be useful to do more at uni, to prepare you for coming here or do you think that there's enough health and safety training once you get here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Health and Safety training here, they're ok but at uni I don't really see a lot of health and safety going on. Before we go to the labs, like before we start to operate on the (pilot plants?) they don't seem to tell us how you have to be careful with them and unless it’s like really important. Like here even if you go up the stairs you have to hold the handrail.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok do you think they should do more health and safety at university then or do you think it doesn't matter?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It's better to explain about health and safety before you operate the plant, but like going up the stairs I don't think is relevant.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the university could have done more to prepare you for coming on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: To help prepare me? I think because I didn't know before I accepted the place that I would actually be doing this kind of job and I asked my supervisor the other day, because they were interviewing my replacement for next year. (Ok) So I asked them if they had already seen the job description before they came and they said, “Yes, I'd sent it to them”. but I didn’t have a chance to look at it before when I came, so when I was in the interview then I realised oh this what I'm gonna do. Then when the people, the new students, came for interview I asked them if they'd seen it, they said that they hadn't seen it you know, so I don't whether it's the company's fault or the university's.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. How did you find the transition from being in education student to being at work, was it easy or difficult?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Very difficult for the first month because I'm not used to getting up early. And, because I get a lift in, so I used to work the long hours with this girl that I know, she works from eight to five, which is normal working hours, I'm only supposed to work nine to five. Sometimes she works from eight to half-five, so it's like very long hours for me. At the start I'm not very used to it, but now I've found another lift that comes in at nine to five, but sometime when I have more work I would like to leave later.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, are you looking forward to going back to university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, very. I don't know why maybe because well it's just not every day like coming to work and then only having weekends off, we get a lot more holiday. But, I’d like to be a student again.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you keeping in touch with your friends and things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. What do you think are the main ways that work and university differ?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The main . . .?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: The main differences between being at work and being at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Like being at work, I think I feel - I think I feel more pressurised, like because, all of the work that I've done, it could be very important to the business, so I couldn't afford to make any mistakes. I have to do finances for my supervisor for his projects and they're like in million Euros, so if I like put one zero less, then they're gonna be all different, to draw the graph, second one and then to check for the exit budget, so at uni these things are not that important. They’re very different.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you do anything on your course about finance or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We did process economics where, yes, you look at how you spend. That's quite different from what I'm doing, yes. I think like [name] and most of my classmates I talk to on placement now, I think most of the work they do are more chemical engineering based.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Can you tell me a bit about what [company] do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm [company] sells fuel, they do a lot of different types of fuels, before I came I didn't realise it. They are very active in the F1. F1. Yes and then they have this new fuel, like automated fuel (sales?) are looking into.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And your job involves looking at fuel emissions?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, fuel emissions, also bio-fuels. Just looking, I did erm, for this - there's this new alternative fuel called [name]. At the moment we only have the (pilot plant?) providing the new fuel, the new commercial plant is not gonna be ready until about a few years time and I look at how this - because we have a limited supply of it and it shows it to give really good emissions, like lower particulates, you know, so we look at how we choose which country to sell it. We sold it in Thailand because it's very bad pollution over there. (Yes) And then we sold it in Athens and not the whole of Greece, because we launched it with the Olympics to get like people (lost words) because Olympic games is always for a greener environment. Also we're looking at customers' feedback on that fuel. I helped my colleague to do research to write a report on all the customers' feedback on the new fuel.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is a lot of your time spent in the lab?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I don't really do any lab work compared to with the other students here who spend all day in the lab but for me its more all reports and computer work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Does the company have like a programme or structure that placement students have to follow, like are there targets that you have set?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really, but they do ask us what we want to achieve at the end of the year. It's very good in terms of that we can ask what we want to do, like if you want to get more involved in this certain project that you know of you can ask them for permission and then they’ll try to let you get involved in it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, and you said you've been on quite a few training courses and things.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, and like because I studied chemical engineering I've always wanted to go to [name], the refinery next door and I've been for a few visits there to see how everything works.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok, that sounds good. Do you feel like you do give an appropriate level of responsibility?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think I'm alright, like sometimes when we don't have enough work to do, you can go around and ask for it, then you can help people, so that's alright, and when I have too much work I can just tell my supervisor what other works I have and can I do this first.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you have got quite a good relationship with your supervisor? He's quite approachable?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, and because they put me in the same room as him, so it' easier when I want something I just ask. They used to employ two students for my placement every year but this year we've got one, But because, they said it's good to have two they said because I can talk to the other students and discuss if I don't know anything or if the others or if the other student's better at doing something, so this year it's a bit harder but not too bad.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Do [company] employ a lot of women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it's more men.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: In your section is it mostly men?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, in my section it's the fuel [name] so yes, the majority are men.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. How would you summarise your placement experience so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I would think it's a good and different experience.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would you say have been the best and the worst things about it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The best thing - I don't think it's happened yet. When I finish my dissertation and be of more use to the company. Yes, it's not like I don't know want them to choose a title for me and then finish [inaudible] and didn’t help them in any way. The worst is maybe understanding emissions and fuel specifications. I think it's quite hard, because I have to go and visit the legislation websites and they're quite boring. I don't do any calculations that I do in uni, just more reading and understanding.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Can it be a bit tedious sometimes?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, but its good practice.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has the placement met your expectations? Is there anything that you thought you would achieve but haven’t done yet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I would like to do more chemical engineering work like but that would be totally different from what I'm doing, so I don't think I'll be able to do that this year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What would you say now are the benefits of doing a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Getting to know people, to know how to communicate with different people, different age groups and also working is a totally different environment to studying.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that'll help you when you go out into the workplace when you've finished university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I think there's one more thing as well. When they interview my replacement, they include me in their discussion like what do they want from this student and what do they think about that? So I can see from that point of view what the interviewers actually want to get out of the student. So that would help me, I think, when I actually go and find a job.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think there are any drawbacks to doing the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really. Despite the work is different from my degree but the other things are really good like you don't find a placement where you get mostly like a free lunch and a gym and a library. But there's also one more thing that this is quite far from town, like if you don't have a car like I don't, so it's really hard to come into work and to get a lift. Sometimes when you want to work later or you want to go to the gym you can't go because you have to get a lift. They don't do like a shuttle bus for the employees. That's one bad thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you find moving to [town], was it difficult to begin with moving to a new place?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It was not too bad, because I studied at [town] before I came to [university], so I moved from [town] to [town], so you get used to it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you’re used to moving round?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you have changed personally from doing the placement, like more confident or independent, things like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I think it's sort of good practice for me to be speaking lots of English because I’m from Malaysia, you don't usually speak English like every day, every hour, this is good practice. And I think if I just go on to uni after my second year I won't see things like how I see things now.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you recommend that other people did a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes I would.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you recommend that people to do the placement that you're doing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It depends what they want to do after their uni and there are a lot of chemical engineer graduates in my department, they chose to do this work as in, it's also very technical but just like nothing to do with like walking around the refineries. It depends on the people.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is it a quite specialized area that you're in at the moment then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I spoke to my colleague, and she's a chemical engineer but she chose to work here. I asked her why she says its because she, it's very complicated at the refinery, like if you're a new starter, a new chemical engineer, you have to deal with operators, sometimes you want to change the way they operate but they won't listen and then you have to deal with it. That's why she chose to work and do research on, it's also on the products on what the refinery has produced but it's like a different side.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. You said that there were some other students on placement here I think?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes but - no. I think that it's only two are of like fifteen those are the students, pre-university students, doing like a gap year. So there's only me and another girl who’s from Scotland.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you're treated equally, or the same as other placement students?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I think so yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it's an advantage or disadvantage having other students on placement at the same time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It's an advantage because I have friends of my own age, at nearly my own age, and then all the students have lunch together, because we don't work in the same department we don't see each other in the day, so it's good to have lunch with different people and then work with different people, get to know more people.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you support each other?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, yes, we do have like social gatherings you know, go out to the cinema.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok that's good. Do you think that you’re treated the same as the permanent members of staff? Or are you treated like the student?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, we are sometimes, it depends on the work, like most of the time I am sort of treated like one of the permanent workers but some other times, like there was this bio fuels meeting that was on and my supervisor wanted me to go on it but then the speaker didn't allow me to go in it. He said, 'We don't allow students, we only allow [company] employees and then my supervisor didn't realise that, and she came and told me that they were talking about very confidential things about the company, about their findings and they didn't want to include me, so that's the difference sometimes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that frustrating?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, it is a bit yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I think that confidentiality is a big issue for quite a lot of companies that interview some students working at [company] and they couldn't really tell me much about their jobs because of confidentiality (Alright) They weren't allowed to tell much about the company. But it's all confidential anyway.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes but most of them, like if there's a talk or if there's a presentation, usually we do get to go.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you had to do a lot of group or teamwork or is it mainly working by yourself?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: My supervisor did like a customer's report on that new fuel that we were supposed to do and he paired me with a colleague and we were supposed to do it together, which was good and now he has a new project and he paired me with a different colleague.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. How do you think doing group work at work compares with doing group work at university? Is it easier or harder?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: At university there is usually – there’s not much of a difference. There's bigger groups of people working on the same thing, but here I've only been like in a group of two people. It’s not much of a difference, unless like in university you meet people who doesn’t do work like in a group, it's frustrating like that but here I don't think that's gonna happen because everyone is here to work or maybe they love their job, that's why they're here.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that doing group work at university is beneficial for when you're doing group work here? Do you use skills from it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I do yes, like at uni, when you do group work you have to like listen to people's ideas and like try to accept it and it's the same as here as well, just listen and then you have to provide your own ideas if that's not done in group work at uni I might not know about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Have you particularly liked or disliked working with any people here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really - no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So it's just been okay?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you been given a mentor at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No - mentor - are they the same as supervisors?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Well sometimes I think a lot of people that haven't specifically been given a mentor see their supervisors as a mentor, but a mentor might be someone different, somewhere else in the company that you can just go and talk to about general things, if you had any problems or career advice or anything like that.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There are different people for different things here, if I want, it depends, if I want to talk about a health and safety problem I could see a representative, or if I want to do some research in IT, there's an IT representative, I haven't got anyone that's especially assigned to me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: If you need any advice or anything like that you would see your supervisor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, my supervisor and the colleagues that I work with, that he paired me with, I know them as my friends as well, so I can talk to them.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, so they’re quite supportive, ok. Is there anyone else in the company or anyone in the company that you think of as like a role model?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think one of the colleagues who I work with, she's a chemical engineer and she's only started like 6 months before me but when I came she's like catch up everything like that's going on really, she's been adapting really well and like understanding like all the different jargons that they use here - and every time I talk to her, because if I don't understand any work, she works for my supervisor, so if I don't understand any work that I'm doing I can just go to her and ask her and she'll explain it very clearly to me, so like talking to her sometimes like inspires me to work more hard, do more research. She's like a role model.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has anyone from the university been to visit you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, no because I go back to university quite often. (Ok) So no, they've not been here to visit. My friends has been.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But not a placement supervisor or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh yes, placement supervisor, he's been here once, once to visit me in September, that's two months after I started, he says he'll come about three times a year.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. What sort of things did they talk to you about?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They talked to me about like how am I getting on and what other work that I do, he asked about my dissertation, how much time I allocate to do it a week and who are my supervisors who are looking after - because I have a different supervisor who looks after the dissertation.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you know the person that came to visit you before? Did you know the person that came to visit?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The lecturer? Yes. As in the name?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Had they taught you at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Did they speak to your supervisor as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, I think they did spend some time with my supervisor and some time with me alone and with all of us.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you find it helpful having that visit?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It could be helpful if I had problems then I could talk to him more than my supervisor, but I find my supervisor quite friendly, so I can talk to him.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So if you had any problems, you'd try and sort it out at work first before you went to your placement tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Are you in contact with the person at university, when they're not visiting you, do they email you or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They don't really, no. I email him every month to send him the monthly report, I have to send a report every month to say what I'm doing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you be happy to talk to that person if you did have any problems at all? Or is there anyone else at university that you'd rather talk to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Maybe I would rather talk to my personal tutor at uni?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you know whether, either here or at university, if they have like a complaints procedure if you did have any problems at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think there should be but not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Are there appropriate facilities for women here? There's enough women toilets and if you had to wear, you probably don't, but if you have to wear safety clothing and things like that, is it in the right sizes?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh yes, we had to do this fire fighting training where we had to like put out a fire. We had a red one, it was really big, but there are smaller sizes I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Some of the students I’m interviewing are working on building sites and things like that, so they don't necessarily always have like women’s toilets?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The fire extinguisher's so heavy I couldn’t even lift the lightest one, but it's my first time to put out a fire. [laughter]

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That sounds scary.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: There's a properly trained firemen there to look after us - should be ok.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Can you think of any occasions when you think of the fact that you're a woman has maybe determined reactions that you've got from people or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You feel like you're treated equally?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes, yes. I think my supervisor prefers to have a girl student, because maybe the way we talk to people and the guys, I think, would seem a bit rude sometimes maybe.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You mean that women are maybe be better at communicating?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Do you think that your career ambitions have changed since doing the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No I still want to be a chemical engineer.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you know what area of chemical engineering you'd like to go into at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I'd like to work in [name] if I can or I wanted to work for a pharmaceutical company before but now I think a petroleum company, it’s not bad.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you work for [company] then, if you had that opportunity?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you know whether they would let you come back if you wanted to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don't know about that, I don't think so, I think I would have to apply again, because it's different companies, there are different small companies within [company].

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You wouldn't want to work in this area again?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: In the research department?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No - I don't think so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Do you think that doing the placement will help you even if you go into another area?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think the communication skill would help, like knowing that you had to persuade the operators, or trying to make them see the sense of what you're doing. So, I think, speaking to all the different people here I think communication skills will help a lot.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the other section will be more male dominated than it is here or do you think it'll be the same?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It feels more male dominated.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that bother you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You said that the other girl said about it often being difficult trying to get the operators to do things, does that bother you at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don't think so, I think it’s like more challenging and more interesting, to think of different ways [laughter] I'll give it a go.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I have got some questions now that are questions that I asked in the last interview but it's not a test, you see if you get the same answers, just to see if your opinion has changed from having the placement experience. What five words would you use to describe it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It's different - The area I work in or the work that I do?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Both, just like the characteristics of the general type of work that you’re doing.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s - can I say technical? Erm…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the characteristics here would be different from the chemical engineering that you want to go into?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The chemical engineering work also is very technical but it also involves a lot of reading, how you start up the plants and all the procedures. I'm interested to do what the chemical engineers do, so I'll find it more interesting maybe you know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Ok. Do you think that there are any advantages or disadvantages of being a woman in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Advantages - Maybe if you do something wrong they won't penalise you that much. [laughter]

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has that happened to you, or is that just what you think?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s what I think. Disadvantages might be – like some more difficult work, they might like give it to the guys, I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yes, ok. Does it concern you at all that there aren't more women in engineering? Do you think that more women should be encouraged to do engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that they don't?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ah I think I remember my answer now, I think it’s going to be the same. I think because, for me as well like when we were small, women want to be like fashion designers, like all those feminine jobs, I would also like fashion, wear spiky heels and all that to work. But I think in becoming a chemical engineer or engineer, we do still go to work like normal people, like we do quite a lot of work on the computers as well but just like sometime you have to go down to the refineries, you have to wear the safety boots and all but I think it's something different from most people and I think it's good.
